analysis.one_liner: Makes companies pay US taxes on stashed offshore profits immediately when they invert.
analysis.headline: A bill to stop companies from dodging taxes by moving their headquarters abroad died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When an American company 'inverts'—merges with a smaller foreign company and declares the new combined firm foreign—it can stop paying US tax on profits its overseas subsidiaries have built up but never sent home. This bill would require companies that invert to immediately count those accumulated offshore earnings as taxable US income, in the same way already required for certain foreign 'subpart F' income [S2] [S3]. It also broadens the definition of an inversion to catch more deals, lowering the ownership threshold and extending it to a wider set of mergers [S3]. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 115th Congress ended [S5] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would otherwise have to make up the revenue lost when profitable US companies shift their tax home abroad. Domestic companies that stay put and pay full US taxes would also face less competitive pressure to follow suit, since inverting would no longer unlock a windfall on stashed profits.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a company that inverts to immediately recognize the accumulated deferred foreign income of its controlled foreign corporations as subpart F income for the last taxable year before the acquisition—ending the deferral benefit that inversions unlock [S2] [S3].

Widens what counts as an inversion: it moves the relevant date to July 24, 2017, drops the foreign-shareholder threshold from at least 60 percent to more than 50 percent, and disregards one of the existing escape clauses, so more merger structures would be covered [S3].
Applies to taxable years ending after July 24, 2017, so it reaches deals underway when the bill was written [S3].

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations that invert or plan to, and their shareholders, who would owe immediate US tax on profits parked offshore instead of deferring it. Accounting and law firms that advise on inversion structures would lose a line of business.

drawbacks.text: Imposing a large immediate tax bill on inverting companies could push some to restructure in ways that still reduce US taxes, and critics of targeted anti-inversion rules generally argue the better fix is broader international tax reform rather than deal-by-deal penalties [S3].
The bill addresses only companies that invert; it does nothing about offshore profit-shifting by multinationals that stay US-domiciled, so much of the tax base erosion it targets would remain [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill tackles a real and visible tax-avoidance practice, but narrowly. It taxes the accumulated offshore earnings only of companies that invert, leaving untouched the much larger pool of offshore profits held by companies that never leave. Its cost falls entirely on firms choosing to relocate their tax home—a cost an honest supporter would call the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on July 31, 2017, joined by Sens. Durbin and Van Hollen [S1] [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction; that referral was the last action in its history [S5] [S1].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational companies that invert or hold large offshore profit piles, and the tax advisors who plan such deals, are better off because the bill never advanced—they kept the deferral benefit the bill would have ended.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Inverting multinationals and their tax advisors

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited two Senate cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the rest of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All three supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Republican-chaired Finance Committee gave it no action.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations that invert or hold deferred foreign earnings
industries.note: The bill would immediately tax their accumulated offshore profits upon an inversion, removing the main financial payoff of relocating a tax home abroad. That revenue otherwise goes untaxed, leaving ordinary taxpayers to cover the difference.

industries.industry: Accounting and law firms advising on inversions and offshore structures
industries.note: The bill narrows the planning space: by sweeping more deals under the inversion definition and taxing deferred earnings at the acquisition date, it reduces the value of the restructuring advice these firms sell.

industries.industry: Domestic companies that pay US taxes without inverting
industries.note: They would face less pressure to follow competitors into inversion deals, since the tax benefit of leaving would largely disappear.
